title: Refactor only behind a golden-frame test
lesson: Before changing engine code, render a fixed set of frames (including motion-blur frames and every scene) from a frozen snapshot and from the new code, and require pixel-identical output.

title: Caption outputs are byte-identical after refactors
lesson: Rebuild words.js, SRT, VTT, script, and transcript from the same inputs and compare bytes before accepting a captions change.

title: Audio mix refactors must be sample-identical
lesson: Run the old and new mix scripts on the same committed stems and require identical samples before replacing the mixer.

title: A test that compares zero files must fail
lesson: Every comparison test asserts that it found things to compare. In zsh, pass lists as arrays (unquoted variables do not word-split).

title: Key every layout off the caption band
lesson: Place titles and key graphics relative to CAP.y (captions sit in the upper third on vertical and the lower third on horizontal) and check a contact sheet for collisions; automatic checks miss overlaps.

title: Decorations leave with their parent
lesson: An accent line, badge, or rule fades out with the text it belongs to, before the next element lands in its space.

title: Pin an engine copy inside each project
lesson: Copy the engine into every new project with its version, so a delivered video can always be re-rendered exactly, even after the engine improves.

title: Study a live session without touching it
lesson: To learn from a project another session is editing, export a committed snapshot (git archive <commit>) instead of reading or copying its working tree.

title: Halftone breaks up small type: print documents plain, draw their words crisp
lesson: A halftone turns type under about 60 px into unreadable dots. Halftone photos only; print documents and line art plain, and draw their words as real text on top so they stay legible and textcheck can see them.

title: Start slides just off-frame: spring overshoot scales with the travel
lesson: A spring overshoots by a share of the distance it travels. Start a slide just outside the frame (not a fixed long distance) and damp it (about .75), so paper settles with a few px of bounce.

title: Re-run the text check after moving a piece into the shared library
lesson: Turning a one-off drawing into a shared, parameterized piece changes its layout math. Re-render the frames that use it and run textcheck before and after the move.

title: Describe videos as specs; keep layouts in beat kinds
lesson: A video described as beats in plain text (video.toml), with facts written as fact:<id>, needs no scene code: layouts live once in beat kinds (beats.js) and every future video reuses them. This is the path to staff-made videos without Claude.

title: On tall frames, stack timelines top to bottom
lesson: A left-to-right timeline wastes a 9:16 frame: four steps end up small and crowded with alternating labels. On tall frames list the steps top to bottom (a dot and line on the left, the date big, the label under it); keep the horizontal timeline for wide frames.

title: In hard-cut beats, pieces hold until the cut
lesson: When beats meet in a hard cut, keep every piece fully visible until the cut; a fade-out just before the cut flashes an empty frame (a blink). Let the next beat's pieces arrive on the clean frame instead.

title: A transition paints the leaving picture itself; the leaving beat stays out of those frames
lesson: When a transition draws the old picture into its own layer, suppress the old beat's own draw for the frames the move covers, or the picture is painted twice: the text log then sees the old words twice and reports false overlaps, and a translucent move ghosts the frame.

title: An async seek must be awaited by every caller, including the text log
lesson: If seek() becomes async (preload hooks for large per-frame images), every page.evaluate that reads state after it must await it, or the state is read before the frame is painted and the check passes on an empty log.

title: A page error at load gives blank frames while render.py exits 0
lesson: Fail a render when the page logs an error during load or seek: Chromium keeps painting the clear colour, so a broken script produces a whole video of empty frames and every exit code is 0.

title: Nested cue words resolve in order, and a plain cue word is the stable form across cuts
lesson: Resolve the cue words inside a beat (list items, bubbles) in order from the beat's own cue, and start the next beat's search after the last of them; write cues as plain words (the search runs forward from the previous cue) rather than word#n, because the nth occurrence changes when a cut keeps only some sentences.

title: The whip's ghost copies must reach a solid picture at the end of the move
lesson: In a blur whip, make the first ghost copy fully opaque as the move settles (and fully opaque at the start of the smear-out); with uniform ghost alphas the frame after the move averages a translucent picture under motion blur and never reaches the final colour.

title: A project's pinned engine copy must be refreshed before a dry run
lesson: A project folder carries its own copy of the engine (new_project.py); after engine fixes, copy core, tools, templates and docs into the project (rsync) before testing there, or the test runs the old code and reports fixed bugs as still present.

title: With a host file and no --narration, the lavalier WAV is the clock, never the camera track
lesson: When the one command gets a camera file, take source/narration.wav (the lavalier) as the narration whenever it exists and only fall back to the camera's own track; the camera track is late by the sync offset, so type lands early and the Whisper check fails.

title: A stand-in narration fails the explainer gates by design; the dry run proves the pipeline, not the pace
lesson: A dry run that uses a faster stand-in recording (206 wpm) with the real spec's cue words makes beats hold 10 s or more and trips the pace, word-cap and still-run gates. Read those three failures as the stand-in's, not the engine's; the proof is the clean text check, the clean key, the sync confidence and a mastered mix. Only the real recording at 150 wpm can pass the gates.

title: Tall frames need their own type layout, not the 16:9 one scaled
lesson: On a 9:16 frame the bottom 420 px and the right 120 px of the lower half are the platform's controls. A scene label sits at .76 of the height (not .93), a claim card is narrower (.74 of the width) and higher (.36), and long hero lines wrap. Check with textcheck rules 1 and 4 on the vertical cut before any review; the 16:9 layout is never a crop (D-044).

title: A phrase card over a short sentence lands as one block (by_word = false), or the 2.5 s hold fails
lesson: With by_word on (the default), each on-screen word lands on the next spoken word, so a 7-word card over a 6-word sentence lands its last word on the next sentence and the beat ends 0.6 s later; the hold rule (L-055) stops the build. For a card whose words are more than about half the spoken words of its sentence, set by_word = false: the block lands on the cue and holds the whole sentence. List items with their own cue words need at least six spoken words (about 2.5 s) after the last item's cue.

title: Prove the spec on the script before anyone records (script_check.py)
lesson: A spec can look complete and still stop the one command on the real words: a cue word Whisper never writes, a card over 8 words, a hold under 2.5 s, a cut over its word cap. tools/script_check.py times SCRIPT.md at 150 wpm (and 120 and 165), splices the shorter cut's words and builds every cut without rendering; the recording needs no further building only when it says so for every spec (video.toml and video-host.toml).

title: Type never crosses a figure of the scene: the label moves, and the text check sees figures
lesson: A scene label under the set at .93 of the height (or .76 on a tall frame) crossed the seated figure's legs on 16:9 and its head on 9:16, and the text check could not see it because figures logged no box. Now every figure logs its box (scene.js figureBox), the label tries its band, the top band and then the free side, and textcheck rule 7 fails any text through a figure. Give label_x / label_y / label_align in the spec to place a label by hand.

title: A test file nobody registers in run_all.py never runs
lesson: Register every tools/test_*.py in tests/run_all.py the day it is written. The suite now fails, naming the file, when a test file on disk did not run.

title: Motion blur never samples across a hard cut
lesson: Sub-frames for motion blur must stay on the frame's own side of a hard cut. Otherwise one frame at every cut blends the two shots (a one-frame double exposure).

title: Metrics are hints: never tune a film to its checks
lesson: Automated checks catch defects; they do not make a film good. Never add motion just to beat a stillness detector, and always pair the numbers with a look at real frames against the storyboard.

title: Prove order independence: render frames forward and reversed
lesson: Render a sample of frames in order in one page and in reverse across several pages; they must match exactly. Hidden state (caches, lazy setup, ctx.filter on the GPU) shows up as a mismatch.

title: Check text along its path, not only at rest
lesson: Models lay text out for its final position, so text collides with other elements while it moves. Check overlaps during entrances and exits too.

title: Hand every cut over through a moving object; never repeat a transition twice running
lesson: Each transition passes through something already in the outgoing shot (a match, push, iris, or morph), its edge belongs to the outgoing style, and the same transition never runs twice in a row. Generic wipes read as filler.

title: Use the worst-case vertical safe zone across TikTok, Reels, and Shorts
lesson: At 1080x1920 keep critical content inside top 96, bottom 340, left 24, and right 132 px, and aim for the comfortable zone: top 168, bottom 496, left 72, right 176.

title: Run parallel critics with different lenses on the real render
lesson: Give the rendered film to several independent reviewers at once, each with one lens (story and message, motion and layout, trust and facts). One reviewer misses what a panel catches.

title: Turn each piece of feedback into a one-line rule
lesson: Record feedback verbatim, turn each note into a one-line imperative rule in the right place (TASTE.md or a template), and consolidate the list when it passes about 15 new entries.

title: Keep other creators' films out of the build context
lesson: Feed Claude your own approved style, but keep other creators' films out of its context, or it reuses their characters, sets, and beats. Study references in a separate step and record only what to borrow.

title: Keep every footage window clear of the cuts inside its source
lesson: Before placing a window of real footage, find every cut inside the source film with a detector that also sees cuts between shots of the same tone, and keep each window's start and end at least 3 frames clear of them. Otherwise the source's next shot flashes up for a few frames.

title: Keep a footage-usage registry so no source span is used twice
lesson: Record every span of source footage the edit uses (file, in, out) in one registry, and refuse a new window that overlaps a used span unless the storyboard marks it as an intended callback.

title: Scan the finished render for short shots and repeated shots
lesson: After the final render, find every cut in the master and list each shot's length and a fingerprint of its frames. Flag any shot shorter than the project's minimum (2 s in his documentary) and any shot that repeats an earlier one, unless the storyboard allows it.

title: Recent facts need a fresh human check before release
lesson: Mark facts that change over time (status, counts, titles, records, 'only' and 'first' claims, anything from the last year) as volatile. A named person re-checks each volatile fact in the week of release; neither a model critic nor the model's own memory can clear one.

title: Show a death through what is missing, never the event
lesson: When a piece reaches a death or a tragedy, show what is missing (the empty place, the object left behind, the name), never the event itself. Do not hold one shot long or cut to a blank screen while the narration carries it.

title: Review renders on a page where notes attach to timestamps
lesson: When there are many renders to review, give the reviewer one page that lists each new render automatically, lets them pause and type a note at a timestamp, writes each note into FEEDBACK.md, and drops a render from the list once it is approved.

title: Open with praise, then the charge, then the question
lesson: For a persuasive explainer about a person or an event, the reference opens with two or three parallel superlatives before naming the subject, then states the accusations in the accusers' own words, then asks the one question the piece will answer. For CFC, a superlative is an 'only' or 'first' claim: use one only as a reviewed fact, or keep the adopted number-or-date hook and move the superlatives to the second beat.

title: Display type lands on the spoken word, one accent per card, lines sized into a block
lesson: Key type outside captions should land on its spoken word (phrases word by word, lists line by line), hold 2.5 to 9 s, carry one accent colour per card, and size each line so the block reads as a rectangle. Drive it from the word file, never from typed seconds.

title: Change the whole picture with a push, wipe or blur whip, and vary the kind
lesson: In a narrated explainer, change scenes with short directional moves (push, slide-in, organic wipe, blur whip, zoom-through, iris, a carried-over element) of 5 to 50 frames rather than hard cuts, and never run the same kind twice in a row. Keep hard cuts for real footage.

title: Keep the host off centre and leave a third of the frame for type
lesson: When a host is on camera, frame them left or right of centre on a flat single-colour wall and leave the other part empty, so type can sit on the wall itself with no box behind it. A name super is a lower third shown once, and only if R-026 is amended for recordings made for compositing (TC-2 bans standing corner labels).

title: The host is the only still thing: the picture changes about every five seconds
lesson: Keep the picture moving: a scene change, a new line of type, a camera push or a puppet gesture about every 5 s, and let only a live host hold still, except for the planned hush before the key moment (MP-3) and never as constant wiggle (LP-7). Report stillness per segment in the critic's pass.

title: A tight voice over a bed that rests under the end card
lesson: Master the voice tightly (a loudness range near 4 LU), keep the bed a few dB under it, and let the bed go silent under the final card after a last sting; a credit card is where the bed plays alone.

title: Faced cartoon likenesses of real historical people
lesson: The reference draws a face on every character, including the real historical subject, and lets the drawn subject speak his own quote. Rejected for CFC: no synthetic likeness of a real person, living or historical.

title: A map with a route that draws on and a date label makes a claim concrete
lesson: When the story reaches a place and a date, show a real map, draw the route on in time with the voice, drop the place name as it is spoken, and set the date as type on the map. Build it from real geography with the names and dates read from facts.

title: Let the subject answer in his own words: a sourced quote over the writing figure
lesson: Near the turn, give the subject of the piece one sourced primary-source quote, set in a handwriting or italic face, appearing word by word as it is read, over an image of the act of writing. Attribute it on screen and keep the quote in the fact bank.

title: Segment a reference video by transition runs, not cuts, and read 14-frame strips
lesson: To study a video that changes scenes with animated transitions, detect runs of 3 or more high-change frames (two measures merged) instead of hard cuts, then render a labelled strip of about 14 frames across each run so a reader can name the transition and its direction.

title: State the verdict last, in one sentence, after the proof
lesson: Hold the thesis until the proof is on the table: story, the other side, the rebuttals, the rule of judgment, the subject's own words and the social proof come first; then one sentence as a full-frame card; then one line that puts the stake on the viewer; then the brand.

title: One wall colour and one accent for the whole piece
lesson: Give a narrated explainer one background colour for every host and type frame and one accent colour used for one word or line per card, so emphasis is unmistakable and the piece reads as one voice. Scene illustrations may carry their own palettes.

title: Fine lines vanish on a phone: weight line art for the smallest screen
lesson: Line art drawn at desktop weights loses its hairlines on a phone. Scale line weights by class: outlines 1.45 times, mid lines 1.25, fine lines 1.1, on top of a 1.2 base, and check a phone-size still before approval.

title: Only the door glows: light points the story at one place
lesson: On a night building, light only the opening the story is about (the door, the seal), never every window. A field of lit windows reads as decoration and splits the eye.

title: Line art draws on like a pen: outlines first, rising from the ground
lesson: For line art, log every stroked path on an offscreen canvas and reveal the finished drawing through a mask: heavy outlines first, bottom to top, then mid lines, fine lines, hairlines; fills and glows fade in only after the lines around them. A soft gold point on each moving outline reads as a pen. p = 1 must equal the drawing with no draw-on.

title: Give a draw-on room in the voice, but not so much the narrator waits
lesson: Doubling every building's draw time with long voice pauses made the narrator sound stuck waiting for the drawings. The kept balance: draws at 1.5 times (about 2 s a building, 3.5 s for the Capitol), voice slowed to 0.87 with 0.5 to 0.8 s pauses, each drawing finished 0.5 to 0.8 s before its word. Mark the pauses in the script for the human recording.

title: A figure walks in and stops like a person, on his word
lesson: For a figure who enters and squares up: a short walk (0.76 s here, 1.9 steps a second) that arrives on the word that names him, arms swinging against the legs, the pelvis shifting over the standing leg with the shoulders countering it, a bob highest at mid-stride, the stride fading over the last 0.22 s, then one soft knee dip and a nod. Derive footstep sounds from the same timing.

title: A no-music version needs a softer effects set, not the same one
lesson: Effects mixed to sit under a score sound loud and electronic once the score is gone. For the no-music master drop the noise whooshes and the reverse swell, roll the hits off above 2.2 kHz (2-pole low-pass), keep the soft stingers, and set the stem 5 dB down.

title: A name super only while the person is on screen
lesson: Do not float a presenter's name and title over animation when she is not in the frame; it reads as clutter and confuses who is speaking. Her own footage carries her title.

title: A map names only what the story names
lesson: Remove orientation labels (big cities, the ocean) from a story map; label only the places the narration names, as pins.

title: Generic real places from reference photos, viewed and never downloaded
lesson: For a school, gym, finish arch or light tower, look at several reference photos in the browser (nothing downloaded), draw a generic place that is no portrait of a real campus, and size every part from real dimensions (a storey 3.7 m, a window 1.9 m) at the scene's px per metre. Record the proportions in the code comment.

title: A draw-on must log every primitive the drawing uses
lesson: The draw-on reveals only what its instrumented context logged. A primitive it does not log (fillRect, strokeRect, rect, arcTo, fillText, drawImage) pops in at the end instead of drawing on; a drop shadow left out of the mask arrives late. When a drawing uses a new primitive, add it to drawon.js and check a mid-progress still.

title: A title holds long enough to read before anything competes with it
lesson: A short title line ('Bodies do.') needs about 1.35 s fully on screen; the next text element (a name super) starts only after it has gone, never during its fade.

title: Tools that cannot run code get exported drawings
lesson: Riverside, Descript and Canva cannot run the engine. Render every reusable drawing to a transparent PNG at 2x (and a traced SVG) with tools/export_drawings.py, keep them in engine/exports/ with a README and a licence row, and point staff there.

title: Load the taste profile and rejected list at intake
lesson: Read TASTE.md, including the rejected list, before proposing a concept, palette, figure style, or music. State in the brief which defaults apply and which questions are open.

title: Ask for every approval at intake, in one batch
lesson: List every download, install, and license decision the build will need in the first reply, with file, source, size, and license, and ask for all of them at once. A late approval request stalls the whole pipeline.

title: End card: one ask, the CFC URL, an optional campaign URL, held 4 s
lesson: End with one ask ('Reach out'), CaliforniaFamily.org, and, when a campaign applies, its URL in the campaign's color. Hold the card 4 s after the last spoken word.

title: Read the event's invitation, theme, and program
lesson: For a video shown at someone else's event, read the invitation, the event page, and the program before storyboarding. Carry the event theme into the end card if it fits, and note every other video or testimony on the program.

title: Put the hook in the first 3 seconds
lesson: Make something meaningful happen in the first 3 seconds, with big text early for sound-off viewing, and use that moment as the cover frame.

title: Check for real testimonies before showing a composite
lesson: Before showing a composite character, check the program and campaign for real testimonies. If the composite echoes a real person who will be present, change the narration, and add one line of grace for people who made the other choice.

title: Use the organization's own words for its services and history
lesson: List a partner's services and history in the partner's own words from its own pages. Never list a service it only refers out, and never claim more than its own copy claims.

title: Make the recorded voice the clock
lesson: Transcribe the narration with word timings, correct the words against the source's own captions, and time every caption, cut, and sound to the spoken words.

title: Build slack into live-narration scripts
lesson: For live narration, write about 155 words per 92 seconds, give every block a few seconds of slack, and tell the speaker which sentence to drop if he falls behind.

title: Measure signal-to-noise at every voice-processing stage
lesson: Measure the noise floor and signal-to-noise ratio before and after each voice stage. Denoise first with a non-local-means filter, then gate, EQ, and compress, and keep a stage only if the ratio does not fall.

title: Use real narrators only
lesson: Use the real narrator's recording or live narration. Never synthesize or alter a real person's voice, and never use macOS system voices.

title: Chunk captions 2 to 4 words with a whole-script optimizer
lesson: Cut captions into chunks of 2 to 4 words, each on screen at least 0.5 s, with a whole-script optimizer that penalizes breaks across commas, before sentence ends, and on weak words.

title: Make caption color follow the background every frame
lesson: Compute caption ink from the background tone at every frame, with a halo that strengthens through mid-tones. Never pick one color per phrase.

title: Color key words by meaning
lesson: Color key caption words by one fixed meaning code: pink for girls, blue for boys, red for danger or the lie, aqua for help, white on dark scenes.

title: Fix punctuation and block em dashes before the first render
lesson: Convert straight quotes and apostrophes to curly ones in every viewer-facing string, and fail the build on any em dash, before the first full render.

title: Load every font before the page reports ready
lesson: Await document.fonts.load for every face and weight, then document.fonts.ready, before setting the flag the renderer waits for. Confirm each face with document.fonts.check.

title: Hold on-screen text at least 2.5 seconds
lesson: Hold every label and on-screen text at least 2.5 s. If the narration moves on sooner, let the caption carry it and log the exception.

title: Cut labels that do not earn their place
lesson: Remove decorative text (signs, building names, corner tags) unless the story needs it. Extra text clips, competes with captions, and adds facts to defend.

title: Keep key content inside platform safe zones
lesson: On vertical social video, keep key content above y 1500 and left of x 960. For projection, keep text at least 110 px from the edges and tell the operator 'fit, not fill'.

title: Check every scene for collisions and edge cuts
lesson: Render a contact sheet for every scene and look for text over busy background, figures cut by the frame edge, and motion that enters the caption band. Fix each before building the next scene.

title: Use the host organization's brand for the host's story
lesson: When a video tells a host organization's story and ends in its ask, build it in that organization's colors, fonts, and design language, taken from its current site and logo files.

title: White-forward CFC palette with red and aqua as meaning accents
lesson: Default CFC scenes to white or daylight. Use CFC red for danger and the lie, aqua only where it means help or protection, navy for adults and text, and gold in support. Keep one or two dark scenes for contrast.

title: Place hard cuts between motion-blur sample windows
lesson: When motion blur averages sub-frames, place each hard cut so no frame's sub-samples straddle it.

title: Give figures weight: anticipation, settle, and staggered holds
lesson: Start actions with anticipation and a drive, end arrivals with an ease-out and a settle, and give idle figures staggered weight shifts that hold between moves. Never use constant wiggle.

title: Move the whole set as one layer on a camera tilt
lesson: Move the whole set as one layer on a camera tilt or pan. Per-layer parallax on a tilt makes back layers lag and pop out.

title: Keep visual metaphors dignified, not literal
lesson: Show a metaphor as a physical, dignified action. Do not act out a phrase word for word.

title: Draw people as shaped silhouettes with no faces
lesson: Draw every person as a shaped silhouette: neck, chest, waist and hips, tapered limbs, hands, shoes, a hair cap, and a kit or trousers. Keep no faces.

title: Keep figure groups readable
lesson: When figures stand in front of another figure, draw them in story order and space them so no figure covers another's silhouette.

title: Route dark-to-light crossfades through a hue
lesson: Never cross-dissolve straight between a dark and a light scene, because the midpoint is muddy gray. Route the background through a color ramp (navy, wine, gold, white) or cut on a word.

title: Cut on a word instead of a short double exposure
lesson: Cut hard on a spoken word when two scenes share no match. A short cross-dissolve between unrelated scenes reads as a double exposure.

title: Draw real places from open map data
lesson: Build place maps from real OpenStreetMap streets and building outlines, show the openstreetmap.org/copyright credit, and send no email address in any map request.

title: Add restrained, local, text-free background detail
lesson: Give backgrounds California-specific, text-free detail at low contrast so they add depth without competing with the figures or captions.

title: Make every stat label true on its own
lesson: Write every on-screen number with its subject, unit, and basis, so a screenshot of that frame alone is true.

title: Never show false intermediate states
lesson: Do not count numbers up through false values, and do not wipe key words on letter by letter. Fade or scale in the final value or the whole word.

title: Start every bed from a real piano recording plus a light ambient layer
lesson: Start each CFC music bed from a simple, emotive solo-piano recording under CC BY or public domain, fitted so its own rest lands on the key moment, with a harmony-following ambient layer under it. Keep a silent version as the fallback.

title: Do not ship a fully synthesized melodic score
lesson: Take melody from a real recording or from real sampled instruments. Keep synthesis to pads, air, bells, and the ambient layer.

title: Keep strings, synthetic voices, and complex classical out of beds under narration
lesson: Under a voice, avoid string quartets, solo strings, and string orchestras. Never use synthesized voices, choirs, or formant pads. Avoid busy classical pieces and tunes the audience will recognize.

title: Fit the music's breath and lift to the key moment
lesson: Score every candidate start offset from the loudness curve: steady before the key moment, a dip into it, a lift after it, a phrase start at 0:00, and a rest under the end card. Then fine-tune the offset so the lift lands on the frame.

title: Let the music come to rest under the end card
lesson: Resolve the music and let it rest in the last seconds: about -42 LUFS short-term under a live-narration end card, or one final chord ringing out on social.

title: Screen candidate recordings before fitting them
lesson: Before fitting a recording, measure its share of energy in the 1 to 3 kHz speech band, scan for applause, check its bandwidth, and confirm its metadata. Dip about 3 dB at 2.5 kHz in any bed under a voice.

title: Keep synthesized parts bright, not muddy
lesson: Measure the power-weighted spectral centroid of every synthesized stem. Aim for 700 to 1500 Hz, with real content up to 8 to 10 kHz and the sub 15 to 20 dB under the pads.

title: Avoid the synthesis and assembly traps that cause clicks and crashes
lesson: Start every envelope release from the level the attack actually reached, never delay a channel with np.roll (it wraps the tail to the front), and clip every slice to a common length before adding. Scan the decoded audio for clicks.

title: Give shrinking-step loops a floor and a cap
lesson: Give any loop whose step shrinks by a factor a minimum step and an iteration cap.

title: Derive sound events from the picture's own motion
lesson: Compute every footstep and impact time from the scenes' own motion exports, and re-export the events after any motion change, so the sounds stay on the feet.

title: Add subtle, motivated foley
lesson: Add subtle, story-motivated sound effects synced to motion: footsteps by surface, ball hits, room tone. For pressure scenes, use synthesized whispers with no words. Duck all of it under the voice.

title: Parse the last ebur128 loudness value
lesson: Read integrated loudness from the last 'I:' line of ffmpeg's ebur128 output, never the first. Check that a mastered score has a loudness range above 2 LU.

title: Use loudness targets by use: -16 LUFS social, -27 LUFS live bed
lesson: Master social video to -16 LUFS integrated and -1 dBTP, with the bed about 12 dB under the voice. Master a bed under live narration to -27 LUFS, and always ship a silent version with it.

title: Fail the mix if the bed ever covers the voice
lesson: Duck the bed under speech with a look-ahead gate, and fail the build if any speech window has the bed within 3 dB of the voice.

title: Encode HD with the BT.709 matrix and tags
lesson: Convert RGB frames to H.264 with the BT.709 matrix and write BT.709 tags. Verify with ffprobe and by decoding one frame against its source PNG.

title: Make every frame a pure function of time
lesson: Draw every frame from seek(t) with no CSS transitions, requestAnimationFrame, clock reads, or unseeded randomness. The same t must give the same pixels.

title: Multiply globalAlpha; never assign it
lesson: In canvas code, multiply ctx.globalAlpha by an element's opacity. Never assign it, or the element ignores its scene's fade.

title: Start every final render from an empty frames folder
lesson: Delete the frames folder, or use a new one, before any final render. The renderer skips frames that already exist, so a 'final' can silently ship old frames.

title: Fail fast on page errors
lesson: Attach page-error and console-error handlers before loading the page, and fail on the first error during boot instead of waiting out the ready timeout.

title: Check tool versions at intake
lesson: Check tool versions and modules at intake and use current flags. This Mac's ffmpeg dropped -vsync (use -fps_mode); Whisper exists only as a command-line tool; librosa and soundfile are not installed.

title: Avoid shell and pipeline traps
lesson: Quote globs in zsh, run scripts from the project root with paths resolved from the script's own file, give every parallel job its own temp name, and pass numeric arguments as separate words.

title: Use static grain only
lesson: Use a static dither texture to prevent gradient banding. Never animate grain.

title: Run an adversarial review before shipping partner-facing work
lesson: Before the final render of anything that carries another organization's name, run two independent reviewers: correctness against the organization's site, social media, filings, and emails, and blast radius on the day. Check each objection against the source and label it BLOCKER, WARN, or REFUTED.

title: Use Whisper on the final mix, compared with its mishearings of the raw
lesson: Transcribe the final mix with Whisper to catch masking, and compare it with Whisper's transcript of the raw narration. Never change correct captions to match Whisper.

title: Look at every second of the finished file
lesson: Decode the finished file with the BT.709 matrix and look at a frame for every second, plus strips around every transition, before delivery.

title: Automate the rules audit
lesson: Audit every delivery against the research rules and the locked decisions, item by item, and fix or log each one. Automate every item a machine can check.

title: Send a phone preview under 30 MB with every master
lesson: Encode a phone preview under 30 MB (CRF 23, AAC 160k, faststart) and send it with every master, because larger files only show in the desktop app.

title: Name deliverables from a manifest
lesson: Name files '<Event or campaign> - <Title> - <FINAL or WITH x> <WxH>.mp4', never reuse a name for different content, and let tools read a manifest instead of parsing file names.

title: Deliver poster and last-frame PNGs and never start on an empty frame
lesson: Never start the video on an empty frame. Deliver a poster PNG (about 3 s in) and a last-frame PNG, and hold the last frame at the end.

title: Send a venue tech note with every event video
lesson: For any video shown at an event, send a tech note: which version to play, keep the speaker's mic live and on top, roll on cue, hold the last frame, 'fit, not fill', no Google Slides import, PowerPoint set to start automatically with rewind and loop off, a walkthrough test, and a USB copy.

title: Size and contrast text for the room
lesson: For a banquet hall, set body text at 44 px or more at 1080p and keep at least 3:1 contrast for large text and 4.5:1 for small text.

title: Ship caption files, a transcript, and a sources file
lesson: Deliver burned-in captions for social plus SRT and VTT files, a transcript, a FACTS file, and a README that lists every sound source and license.

title: Embed only fonts licensed for video
lesson: Embed only fonts whose license covers video (SIL OFL), with the license file beside them. Do not render with Avenir Next, Garamond, or DIN from the system until CFC confirms the rights.

title: Follow CFC's music licensing rules
lesson: Use only original code-composed music, public-domain compositions in public-domain recordings, CC0, or CC BY with credit. Never use Pixabay, NC, ND, or SA licenses, or any track whose license text you cannot quote from its own page.

title: Credit CC BY music on the end card
lesson: Put the CC BY credit on the end card and in the README. A courtesy credit is fine for public-domain recordings.

title: Research as nobody: no logged-in browsers, no email in requests
lesson: Run research agents logged out, with a generic User-Agent and no email address in any header, URL, or payload.

title: Deliver options in sets of two or three and read his sort
lesson: Offer two or three distinct versions of the element under review, side by side with a comparison page. Treat his Considering and Rejected sort as the strongest taste signal.

title: Freeze and fork before a polish pass
lesson: Before handing a delivered version to another session, tag it in git and clone a fork with no remote. Commit one item at a time, with before and after sheets and a PROGRESS row for each.

title: Write handoffs with locked decisions, rules, a timed list, commands, and traps
lesson: When work moves to a new session or model, write a handoff with the goal, locked decisions, binding rules, a prioritized list with timestamps, exact commands, paid-for traps, and finish steps. Tell the new session to ask only about locked decisions or taste calls.

title: Turn a batch of notes into numbered, committed fixes
lesson: Expect his notes in one batch after he watches. Number them, estimate each in minutes, fix each in its own commit, and show a before and after for each.

title: Wait on long jobs with notifications, not sleep loops
lesson: Run long renders and scores in the background and wait on their completion notice or a monitor loop. Do not chain sleep commands, and do not poll by hand.

title: Review for AI tells before every delivery
lesson: Before every delivery, ask of each frame and sound: would a viewer think AI made this? Remove synthetic voices, synthesized melody, stick figures, glows, count-ups, corner labels, and generic motion first.

title: No decorative glows or particle bursts
lesson: Do not add decorative glows, halos, or particle bursts. Use light only where the story motivates it: the sun, stadium lights, or light breaking through.

title: Map a drum kit by probing every key
lesson: An orchestral kit's key layout is undocumented; play each key alone and record level, ring time and spectral centroid. The bass drum is the low, long, 60 Hz key (36 here); the crash the bright, three-second, 9 kHz key (66).

title: Non-local-means denoise beats the spectral denoiser on a phone narration
lesson: On a 52 kbps phone recording with a 21 dB signal-to-noise ratio, ffmpeg's anlmdn (s=6) gained about 6 dB of signal-to-noise; afftdn gained none at any setting tried. Then an expander on the room tone, a cut at 280 Hz, presence at 3 kHz, air above 6.5 kHz and 2.5:1 levelling. Measure signal-to-noise and the 2 to 4 kHz share after every stage.

title: A presenter's own footage goes into the frame sequence untouched
lesson: When a real person's recording shares the narration's clock, decode its frames losslessly (BT.709 tv range to RGB PNG) straight into the final frame folder before the canvas render; the renderer skips frames that exist, so nothing of ours (vignette, grain, captions, resampling, JPEG) touches them. Verify with a pixel compare against a fresh decode.

title: Hold the caption that starts on a cut until the cut
lesson: A caption begins fading in 0.17 s before its first word. If a hard cut falls on that word, the caption appears for a few frames at the wrong height or over the wrong shot. Give the phrase that starts on a cut an alpha ramp from the cut time, on both sides of every cut, as a rule and not per case.

title: Motion blur and hard cuts apply to live footage too
lesson: A cut into or out of a presenter's footage must also sit between the frame shutter windows ((k + .5) / 30) or the blur averaging blends her with the animation for one frame. Cut a frame or two before a spoken word into her, and on the word boundary out of her.

title: The end card goes after the presenter's last frame, on its own
lesson: With the presenter's footage untouched, the locked end card cannot sit over her. Cut to the card after her last frame and hold it four seconds after her last word; fade its elements in over a quarter second on white.

title: Write the hand-over file before the account can run out
lesson: A team account hit its usage limit three times in two days. Keep a HANDOFF file in the repo (paste-able first prompt, state of every branch, open decisions, rebuild and render commands, traps) and refresh it at every delivery, on every branch, so a session on any account continues without loss.

title: The text check misses text cut off at the frame edge
lesson: Flag any visible text whose box runs past the left or right edge of the frame (x0 < 0 or x1 > W), anywhere on screen. A line that does not wrap is cut off at both edges, and the safe-zone check reports it only where it crosses the right-hand strip in the lower half.

title: HyperFrames Studio app: unusable signed out, full-access agent, self-updating, no licence
lesson: Do not install the HyperFrames Studio desktop app on a CFC Mac. It does nothing until you sign in to HeyGen (banned by L-207), runs your own Claude Code or Codex with 'Full access' by default, updates and restarts itself with no off switch, and its code and licence are not public. Its editor is the same web editor the pinned CLI already serves with `hyperframes preview`; test that instead.

title: HyperFrames editor: timeline moves clips, not animations; its agent tool and Undo can damage a project
lesson: Do not use the HyperFrames editor (the web editor or the Studio app around it) for timing changes on CFC cards. Its timeline drags change only clip start and length, not the GSAP tweens, so beats go blank or pop on. Its agent tool studio_update_animation can rewrite a shared helper and report no change, and its project-wide Undo deletes files written outside the app instead of reverting the bad edit.

title: A quote the narrator does not read lands as one block
lesson: When the narrator says other words while a sourced quote shows, a word-timed quote finishes on an arbitrary spoken word and can leave its attribution too little time to read. Land it as one block on its cue word (by_word = false), and test the timing on a natural-pace scratch voice, not only the script check's 150 wpm model.

title: Write a story style as a spine, freedoms and checks, not a timeline
lesson: Save what makes a video work as a short brief: the few things every such story has (a real voice and face, a named case, one visual code, a picture for every claim, an anchor and one ask), what stays free (scenes, metaphor, camera, scene count), and what is checked after a draft (holds, safe zones, sourcing). A recipe of beats and seconds copied from one good video, or a library of card types, pushes every later video toward the same slides.

title: Land a figure softly: anticipation, an eased descent, the knees take the weight
lesson: A figure that arrives from above reads as a slam when it falls in a few frames with an accelerating ease. Give it a short rise first, a descent of about half a second that slows into the surface, and a knee bend that straightens over a third of a second; move anyone displaced aside with a step, not a knock.

title: A flash must hand over to the light, never back to the dark
lesson: A two-frame white flash cut back to a dark frame reads as flicker (light, dark, light). Fade the flash out over about 0.4 s while the background under it eases quickly toward the light it is announcing.

title: A collapse into an object matches its place, size, shape and moment
lesson: When many figures collapse into the next scene's object, pack them into that object's shape at its exact screen position and size, finish the pack before the object appears, and let the object fade in solid over the pack ahead of its scene's fade.

title: A draw-on for filled art: outline first, then the fill floods up inside it
lesson: In a flat filled style, draw a prop on in two beats: log every filled and stroked shape on an offscreen layer, draw each outline along its edge (nearest the ground first), then flood each fill upward inside its outline and fade the outlines. Keep drop shadows in the mask. Use it only for things that arrive inside a shot, and check the narration leaves the window: here only 0.9 to 1.0 s was free.

title: Start from the idea and let Claude ask the intake questions
lesson: Begin every video with the idea only, and have Claude ask for the goal, the audience, the one action the viewer should take, where it will be published, the length, and the format. Decide the answers together and write them down before any storyboard or code.

title: State length and aspect ratio as hard limits
lesson: Give the exact length in seconds and frames at a stated fps (180 s = 5,400 frames at 30 fps) and the aspect ratio, never shorthand like '90s', and verify them after render. Scene ranges must add up to the total.

title: Use a block-structured brief
lesson: Write every brief in fixed blocks (inputs, perspective, direction with a Banned list, structure, build contract, facts, limits, plan-first start) and keep the technical header locked while only the story block changes.

title: Put a perspective block in every brief
lesson: Tell Claude at the start that the script is intentionally one-sided CFC advocacy and that CFC's positions are in the approved script and position file. Claude visualizes them without adding counterarguments, and flags factual problems instead of softening claims.

title: Hand Claude the tool and asset inventory
lesson: Tell Claude which tools, licensed assets, reference folders, and prior projects exist, where they live, and which ones are off limits. Without an inventory Claude guesses or improvises a stack.

title: Tell Claude to stop and ask when a tool or key is missing
lesson: Write the fallback into every brief: if a tool, file, or key is missing, stop and ask. Do not let Claude improvise a new stack or widen the scope.

title: Brief parallel scene workers with a written animation guide
lesson: Before splitting scenes across subagents, write an animation guide: the requester's direction verbatim, the code contract with a short example, the canvas and reserved areas, what the engine already draws, the helper API with safe ranges and allowed options, style rules, and exact self-check commands. Put CFC's hard rules in an addendum no prompt can override, and keep the story in the storyboard.

title: Name the moment the viewer should feel
lesson: Name the one moment the viewer should feel, the one special effect saved for it, and the exact tone of the last beat. For CFC the ending lands on moral clarity, not ambiguity.

title: Give brand context and references, and say exactly what you like
lesson: Before storyboarding, give Claude the brand kit (logos, fonts, exact hex codes, screenshots, previous work) and two to five references, naming exactly what you like in each: camera movement, animation, pacing, how the subject is introduced. Say references are inspiration, point Claude at a past piece it can open as the quality bar, and keep the script, numbers, and quotes fixed.

title: Keep a render environment of licensed assets on the Mac
lesson: Keep one folder of cleared assets on the render Mac (fonts, logos, approved photos, sample and SFX packs, impulse responses) with a license file per pack. Claude finds and uses whatever is present, so put only cleared material there.

title: Hook in the first 3 seconds with big text
lesson: Put the hook in the first 3 seconds and make its words big on screen, because feeds autoplay muted. The hook must read without sound.

title: End on one ask and one URL, held at least 4 s
lesson: End on one ask, one URL, and a deadline where there is one, and hold the end card at least 4 s after the last word. Use a UTM-tagged link so clicks can be measured.

title: Use documentary grammar for civic explainers
lesson: Build narrated civic explainers from a small kit of documentary scenes: archival stills with slow push-ins, quote cards with attribution, big stat cards with year tags, maps, and timelines. It reads as journalism, not a slide deck.

title: Carry the story with a recurring motif and a rhyming end
lesson: Give longer pieces one recurring motif, protagonist, or set that returns with visible escalation, and end on the opening image, changed.

title: Time every read, one at a time
lesson: List each thing the viewer must understand as a timed read and give each read its own time; if the reads do not fit, lengthen the shot or cut a read, never squeeze. Reveal one new thing at a time and start a reaction only after its cause is seen.

title: Make something happen in every shot
lesson: Give every shot an event (something changes between its first and last frame), one focal action with a clear silhouette, cause before reaction, and a payoff for every setup.

title: Keep a library of proven formats as templates
lesson: Build proven formats as reusable templates (documentary explainer, one-board whiteboard, verse card, hymn story, sacred-space seasonal short, talking-head B-roll, bill status card, silent lobby loop) and start each new piece from the closest one.

title: Alternate dense and calm, and hold the turn
lesson: Alternate dense passages with calm ones, build pressure toward the turn, then give the turn a held beat of about 3 s of darkness or quiet. Calm is not dead time, so cut filler.

title: Approve the script before any animation
lesson: Put most of the effort into the script and get it signed off before voice or animation starts. Code cannot rescue a weak argument.

title: Keep narration near 150 words per minute
lesson: Write about 150 spoken words per 60 seconds and at most 225 words for 90 seconds, and never speed a voice past 1.1x. Fast speech hurts comprehension and caption timing.

title: Leave it out rather than guess
lesson: If a fact is uncertain, leave it out and list it in NOTES.md for a person to resolve, and label any illustrative graphic as illustrative. Never invent a quote, number, date, or statistic, and allow easter eggs only when they are real and sourced.

title: Give history pieces a historian and a slower pace
lesson: Assign a named historian reviewer to any history piece, check the timeline for gaps before recording, and slow the pace. Declare any borrowed tune.

title: Put every on-screen line in the brief word for word
lesson: Write every on-screen line into the brief exactly as approved so Claude places signed-off text instead of writing it; any line Claude improves goes back through sign-off.

title: Make the voice the clock
lesson: Approve the script, record the voice, measure every word's time into one timing table, and only then animate. Derive cuts, captions, and cues from that table; a new voice take retimes its scene and every scene after it.

title: Clean a phone-recorded narration gently
lesson: Treat phone-quality narration with a light chain: high-pass near 90 Hz, gentle denoise, a soft expander on room tone, a cut near 280 Hz, presence near 3 kHz, air above 6.5 kHz, and about 2.5:1 leveling. Never change its timing or pitch.

title: Show 2 to 4 caption words at a time, each at least 0.5 s
lesson: Chunk captions into 2 to 4 words, keep each chunk on screen at least 0.5 s, time it within 80 ms of the voice, and keep each SRT cue line at 84 characters or fewer.

title: Break captions where a reader would pause
lesson: Choose caption breaks with a cost function: never run across a sentence end, avoid crossing a comma, avoid ending on a weak word ('the', 'of', 'to'), and keep one meaning color per caption.

title: Caption from the approved words, not raw speech recognition
lesson: Caption exactly what is spoken: take the words from the approved script, take the timing from speech recognition, and hand-check every mismatch against the audio. Show written forms on screen ('5.5', 'AB 1955') while timing follows the spoken words.

title: Burn captions into vertical cuts and ship SRT and VTT
lesson: Burn captions into every vertical cut and also generate SRT and VTT files from the same word timings for upload. Ship a plain transcript too.

title: Color key words by meaning with a fixed legend
lesson: Give caption key words a small fixed color legend tied to meaning, and keep it the same for the whole piece. Color must add meaning, not decoration.

title: Let caption color follow the background through crossfades
lesson: Compute caption color from the background tone at every frame, not once per phrase, and strengthen the halo through mid-tone transitions. Text must never sit dark on dark or white on light.

title: Bring caption words in just ahead of the voice
lesson: Start each word's entrance about 70 ms before it is spoken, rise and scale it in from 90 percent, and let a key word land 10 percent large and settle over about 0.3 s. Exit the old phrase before the next one enters.

title: Record which speech engine timed the captions
lesson: Record the speech-recognition engine, model, and settings that produced each word-timing file, so caption timing can be reproduced.

title: Hold on-screen text at least 2.5 s and keep it under about 8 words
lesson: Keep non-caption text visible at least 2.5 s and at most about 8 words at once (labels 3 words or fewer), with one big number or sentence plus one label per scene. Hold simple cards 5 to 7 s and complex diagrams 8 to 14 s.

title: Load every font face before the page reports ready
lesson: Load each font face explicitly and wait for document.fonts.ready before the renderer captures a single frame.

title: Capture text crisply: sRGB profile, scale 1, no LCD text
lesson: Launch the capture browser with a forced sRGB color profile, LCD text off, font hinting off, and device scale factor 1. Never put CSS will-change on anything that scales, or the text blurs.

title: Cut text that restates what the viewer already sees or hears
lesson: Keep word-timed captions, but cut labels, signs, and callouts that repeat what the picture or voice already says. Allow a bill-number card, one short sourced phrase per scene, and the end card.

title: Give each font one job
lesson: Use one display family for all type and a second family with exactly one job, such as a serif italic only for Scripture.

title: Keep key content out of the platform overlay zones
lesson: In a 1080x1920 frame keep key text out of the top ~220 px, the bottom ~380 to 400 px, and the right ~140 px, and overlay these zones on review sheets.

title: Give big text a quiet background
lesson: Reserve the caption band in exact pixels in every scene brief and keep faces and key action out of it. Where text is big, keep the background behind it quiet, and reuse 2 or 3 fixed text anchors so text never jumps.

title: Route dark-to-light crossfades through a hue, never gray
lesson: Never crossfade straight between a dark and a light scene; the midpoint turns muddy gray. Route the background through a color (navy to blue to white, or navy to wine to gold to white).

title: Dither gradients with static grain; never animate grain
lesson: Add a faint static grain to dither gradients so the encoder does not band them; never animate it. Build textures once at setup and let no scene add its own.

title: Make every frame a pure function of time
lesson: Compute every pixel from t inside seek(t): no timers, no CSS transitions, no state carried between frames, and seeded randomness only. The same t must always paint the same frame.

title: Keep overshoot tiny and never bouncy
lesson: Use springs and easing curves, never linear for UI-style motion, and allow a tiny overshoot at most. Bouncy easing is banned.

title: Render motion blur from subframes
lesson: Render motion blur by averaging several subframes per output frame across a shutter. It makes fast moves read as motion instead of strobing.

title: Put hard cuts between frames when blur is on
lesson: With a multi-subframe shutter, place a hard cut so no frame's subframes straddle it, or the frame carries a ghost of the old shot.

title: Move, then hold; no constant wiggle
lesson: Give motion a start and an end and let things hold between moves. Idle life (a weight shift, a breath) comes every few seconds, staggered, never as a constant wobble.

title: Move the whole set in a camera tilt; parallax needs a moving camera
lesson: A pan or tilt from a fixed camera has no parallax, so move the whole set as one piece. Use layered parallax only when the camera itself travels.

title: Stagger and offset so nothing moves in lockstep
lesson: Give each limb, figure, and group member its own timing offset, phase, and seed, and stagger group entrances by small fixed steps.

title: Keep the camera alive, and make big moves mean something
lesson: Give most shots a slow push or drift and save big moves (pull back as scale grows, rise to reveal, fly through into the next scene) for meaning. Change shot size when a scene feels static, zoom in log space, and add a decaying shake only on impacts.

title: Build figures on a reusable rig with a pose library
lesson: Draw characters from one skeleton rig with named poses and pose blending, so every scene reuses the same figure and new motion is a new pose, not new drawing code.

title: Shape figures as silhouettes, not stick figures
lesson: Give pictogram figures shaped silhouettes on the skeleton (neck, chest, waist, tapered limbs, hands, shoes, hair cap, kit) in shades derived from the palette.

title: Use anticipation and follow-through in figure motion
lesson: Before a big move, show the load (a set position, a knee bend, arms swinging back); after it, let hair, limbs, and props follow through and settle last. Save squash and stretch and hit-stops for the big beats.

title: Walk cycles need sway, counter-roll, and a settle
lesson: Walks need hip sway over the standing leg, arms swinging against the legs, a shoulder counter-roll, the body highest at mid-stride, a stride that fades out, and a settle at the end.

title: Lock designs and key poses on still sheets before animating
lesson: Approve character, prop, and logo designs, and each shot's key storytelling poses, as still sheets before adding motion. Motion cannot rescue poses that do not read.

title: Plant feet on the drawn ground and drive strides from distance
lesson: Compute foot height from the same function that draws the ground, drive the walk phase from distance traveled so feet never slide, and check each contact with a close-up crop.

title: Grow transitions out of the content
lesson: Give every seam a transition that grows out of something on screen (a pin irises open, a field collapses into a ball, a camera flies through). Allow a plain cut only on action or as a deliberate smash cut, and switch scenes only under full cover.

title: Replace double exposures with a clean cut on a word
lesson: When two busy scenes overlap in a short dissolve, cut cleanly on a spoken word instead. A double exposure reads as a mistake.

title: Hand the eye to the same element across a cut
lesson: Across a cut or handoff, keep the viewer's point of focus on the same or a matching element in the same place and size.

title: Cut on the beat or on a word
lesson: Place hard cuts on a musical beat or a spoken word so the edit feels intended.

title: Add restrained, text-free background detail
lesson: Give empty sets quiet, text-free detail drawn at 7 to 20 percent ink, and keep the frame white-forward so the story stays in front.

title: Draw place-true silhouettes with seeded variety
lesson: Draw scenery that fits the place (coast live oaks, eucalyptus, and fan palms for California) with seeded variety in size and mirroring, not generic circle clusters.

title: Use motivated light only; no decorative glow
lesson: Allow light only when something in the scene makes it, and derive every light effect from one defined source so light and shadow always agree. Drop decorative glows.

title: Paint backgrounds past the frame and build depth with overlap and color
lesson: Paint background planes well past the frame edges so pans, zooms, and shakes never expose an edge, and build depth with overlap, scale, and mixing distant layers toward the sky color.

title: Never show false mid-count numbers
lesson: Do not animate a count-up that shows numbers that were never true. Fade or slide in the final value instead.

title: Read on-screen numbers from FACTS, never type them
lesson: Put every on-screen number, date, name, quote, and verse in FACTS with its source, date, a short quote, and a reviewer field, and have scenes read values from FACTS with a data date on screen. Draft charts with placeholders until FACTS supplies the value.

title: Draw maps from real geographic data and credit it
lesson: Draw maps and scenes from real data (boundaries, terrain, the sun position for the date) with a suitable projection, state any exaggeration, and add any attribution the data license requires.

title: Score only with code-composed or public-domain music
lesson: Use only music CFC composes in code or public-domain scores CFC arranges itself. Keep a music notes file that says how every cue was made.

title: Build the score on a beat grid anchored to the first hit
lesson: Pick a tempo, anchor bar 1 on the video's first big hit, and place chord changes and hits on that grid. Export the tempo and offset from the composer so scenes can place beats as B(n) = offset + n x 60/BPM instead of typed decimals.

title: Brief the score with a cue sheet tied to spoken words
lesson: Write a music brief with the tempo, key plan, and a cue sheet that lists each hit, riser, drop, and lift by time and by the word it lands on, plus hard rules from past feedback.

title: No synthesized voices, choirs, or formant pads in the music
lesson: Keep vocal-like sounds out of the score: no synthesized voices, formant 'choir' pads, or singing textures.

title: Keep code scores bright: centroid 700 to 1500 Hz
lesson: Measure the score's power-weighted spectral centroid and aim for 700 to 1500 Hz with real content to 8 to 10 kHz and sub cut below 30 Hz. Code scores tend to come out muffled.

title: Humanize code-composed music with seeded timing and touch
lesson: Offset each note by a few milliseconds and vary its velocity slightly with a fixed random seed, so the score sounds played but stays reproducible.

title: Carve a pocket for the voice in the music
lesson: Dip the music stem gently (2 to 3 dB) around 1.5 to 4 kHz so the voice sits on top without heavy ducking.

title: Release envelopes from the level reached; never wrap delays
lesson: Release every envelope from the level it actually reached and never use a circular shift for a delay line; both cause clicks and wrapped tails.

title: Iterate the soundtrack as its own pass, with variants
lesson: Treat the score as a separate pass: make two or three variants, compare them side by side, and let the approver choose by ear.

title: Prefer real instrument samples to pure synthesis
lesson: Where the license allows, sequence real instrument samples (a General MIDI soundfont, a cleared sample pack) instead of pure synthesis; they sound less artificial.

title: Render your own performance; do not sample old recordings
lesson: Perform public-domain works yourself: convert ABC, LilyPond, or MusicXML to MIDI and render it through a cleared soundfont or synth. Never use downloaded recordings or unlicensed engravings; only recordings first published in 1925 or earlier are public domain in 2026.

title: Compute sound events from the picture's own motion
lesson: Generate the SFX event list from the same motion functions that draw the picture (a footstep when a run phase crosses a landing mark, a hit at the impact time), with screen x for panning and a level per event.

title: Re-export sound events after any retime
lesson: Whenever a motion is renamed or retimed, re-export the sound events and rebuild the foley stem, or footsteps drift off the feet.

title: Put big hits on motion peaks and key words
lesson: Land the biggest hits where the picture peaks and a key word lands, and keep the rest quieter so the peaks read.

title: Give foley surfaces, alternating feet, and room tone
lesson: Alternate left and right steps slightly in pitch and pan, give each surface its own texture, run interior sounds through a room impulse response, and lay a quiet room tone under interior scenes.

title: Synthesize UI and transition SFX in code
lesson: Make whooshes, clicks, risers, and impacts in code (noise and sine envelopes) so every sound is owned and reproducible.

title: Use licensed sound banks only inside the mix; never ship the files
lesson: Use a licensed sound bank only as mixed into the soundtrack and never distribute the raw files. Do not use macOS 'say' voices in public or nonprofit work.

title: Master to -16 LUFS integrated and -1 dBTP
lesson: Master the final mix to -16 LUFS integrated with a -1 dBTP true-peak ceiling, using a two-pass linear loudness normalization.

title: Keep music about 10 to 12 dB under the voice
lesson: Hold the music bed about 10 dB under the voice while someone speaks, and report the voice-to-bed ratio so no window has the bed louder than the voice.

title: Duck the music with a speech gate
lesson: Drive ducking from a speech envelope with hold and lookahead (about 220 ms hold, 90 ms lookahead, 60 ms attack, 450 ms release) and drop the music about 6 dB and the foley about 3 dB while the voice speaks.

title: Automate the score under key lines
lesson: Step the score back a few dB under the most important lines and let it bloom after the last word.

title: Check true peak after the AAC encode
lesson: Measure loudness and true peak on the final encoded file, not only on the WAV, because AAC encoding raises peaks.

title: Parse the last ebur128 summary, not the first match
lesson: When reading ffmpeg ebur128 output, take the last integrated-loudness match; it prints per-frame values before the summary.

title: Capture frames with headless Chromium through seek(t)
lesson: Render with a headless browser that calls seek(t) for each frame and saves a PNG, then encode with ffmpeg. Serve files through a local route so the page loads nothing from the internet.

title: Review a low-resolution preview before the full render
lesson: Build, then render and review a low-resolution preview before any full-resolution render. Local renders are heavy.

title: Render a few stills per scene before moving on
lesson: After building each scene, render 3 or 4 stills, including one mid-transition, and look at them. Fix layout, overlaps, legibility, and pacing before the next scene.

title: Make renders resumable, and clear frames before a final
lesson: Make renders resumable, write each frame to a temporary file and rename it when complete, and re-render any truncated frame. Clear the frames of an edited shot, or the whole folder before a final, so no stale frame survives.

title: Size render workers to the machine
lesson: Size parallel render workers to the machine (8 on the M1 Pro, 2 to 4 on a MacBook Air, 2 on 8 GB), let each pull the next frame from a shared queue, and log milliseconds per frame and an ETA. Keep laptops awake with caffeinate and keep 10 to 20 GB of disk free.

title: Encode H.264 High, yuv420p, BT.709-tagged, faststart
lesson: Encode masters as H.264 High profile, yuv420p, with BT.709 matrix, primaries, and transfer tags and faststart. Convert RGB to YUV with the BT.709 matrix explicitly.

title: Fail the render on page errors
lesson: Treat any page error or console error during capture as a failed render, not a log line.

title: Multiply globalAlpha, never assign it
lesson: In canvas code, multiply ctx.globalAlpha by a child's alpha; never assign it, or children ignore their scene's fade.

title: Floor step sizes and cap iterations in search loops
lesson: In any loop that shrinks its step, floor the step and cap the iteration count so it always ends.

title: One file per scene on a shared engine, registered by time
lesson: Build each scene as its own file on a shared engine, register it with its time range in one registry, and draw a visible placeholder wherever no scene covers the time.

title: Check contact sheets, strips, and spot frames
lesson: Review labeled grids of stills across each range, strips around every transition, and close-up crops of figures and contacts, and open each image to look at it. Claude cannot watch video; it can only read frames.

title: Save before and after sheets for every change
lesson: Before changing an item, render a sheet of its time range; after the change, render the same times. Keep both images next to the log entry.

title: Run a separate critic with a scoring rubric
lesson: Have a separate critic (a fresh agent) score the render against a written rubric and send it back until every area passes. The builder should not grade its own work.

title: Run an adversarial two-reviewer pre-ship review
lesson: Before anything ships, have two independent reviewers try to refute it (correctness and blast radius). Their blocking items stop the render.

title: Transcribe the final mix and diff it against the script
lesson: Run speech recognition on the final mix and compare it word by word with the approved script to catch dropped words, mispronunciations, and timing slips.

title: Fail the build on any Scripture mismatch
lesson: Compare every on-screen verse with the source text of the named translation and fail the build on any mismatch, including the translation label.

title: Gate delivery on scripted pass/fail checks, and never weaken one
lesson: Run a finalize script with pass/fail checks on size, frame rate, frame count, duration, color tags, pixel format, audio format, loudness, true peak, and Scripture. Never weaken a check to make it pass.

title: Run a claim-extraction pass against the sources
lesson: Have two people check every claim on screen and in the voice against primary sources, show the source on screen and in the post, and recheck bill status the week the piece ships. Ask Claude for its source list to confirm the script is not one article in disguise.

title: Close every piece with a rule-by-rule audit
lesson: Finish with a written audit that walks every locked decision and research rule and marks each PASS, FIXED, or exception with a reason.

title: Have a named Scripture reviewer approve verses and theological claims
lesson: Name a pastor or theologian as Scripture reviewer and have them approve every verse, translation label, and theological claim before release.

title: After the first full cut, rebuild the weakest scenes
lesson: After the first full version, list and rebuild the two weakest scenes, polish second by second, re-pull frames with the safe zones overlaid, and have a person listen on headphones and a phone speaker.

title: Give timestamped, specific feedback and keep it in the project
lesson: Give feedback as time-coded, specific notes ('at 00:03 hold the product screen longer'), including notes on audio. Keep the storyboard, assets, and feedback in the project folder so every revision uses the same context.

title: Ship a poster frame and a last-frame PNG
lesson: Export a poster (cover) PNG and a last-frame PNG from the finished file, decoded with the same color matrix it was encoded with.

title: Make a phone preview under 30 MB
lesson: Produce a phone preview under 30 MB (H.264 CRF 23, AAC 160k, faststart) for review on a phone and remote delivery, and keep the full master separately.

title: Deliver editable source, not just a video
lesson: Keep the code, text, and timing in a versioned repo so staff can change copy or timing and re-render. Editable source answers the 'one-shot needs adjustments' critique.

title: Cut a version per platform and length
lesson: Plan each piece as a set of cuts: a 16:9 master, a 9:16 Reels cut of 20 to 45 s, a 4:5 or 1:1 Facebook cut of 60 to 120 s, a 2 to 5 minute YouTube explainer plus a Short, and X cuts of 2:20 or less. Upload at exactly the platform size with the highest-quality setting on.

title: Require a self-review report with every delivery
lesson: Have Claude deliver the MP4 path, a scene table, a short summary of creative decisions, the changes it made after frame review, what is still rough, what it could not verify (such as 'the mix was not listened to'), and NOTES.md.

title: Target WCAG 2.1 AA with captions, caption files, and a transcript page
lesson: Target WCAG 2.1 AA: caption all prerecorded audio including meaningful non-speech sounds, ship caption files, and publish a transcript page with every on-screen stat and its source, built from the same data as the animation.

title: Measure caption contrast against the frames behind it
lesson: Check caption contrast against the actual pixels behind each caption, not against the palette, and fix any chunk below 4.5:1.

title: Use AI for captions and translation without an AI label
lesson: Use speech recognition for caption timing and AI help for translation without adding an AI disclosure, but keep those uses separate from narration.

title: Never synthesize or alter a real person
lesson: Never create synthetic faces or voices of real people, living or historical, never alter a real person's image or voice, and never give an AI a clergy or real-person persona. A 'This has been manipulated' label does not make it lawful for CFC.

title: Put public-domain Bible text on screen
lesson: Use the BSB (public domain since April 30, 2023) as the English default, or KJV, ASV, or WEBP ('LORD'). For Spanish use Reina-Valera 1909, and RVR1960 only within 500 verses, under half of any book and a quarter of the work, with its notice; verify every translation at its publisher and never copy Bible text bundled inside third-party tools.

title: Copy methods, not code, from unlicensed repos
lesson: Learn from unlicensed or non-commercial repos by restating the method in CFC's words, and copy MIT code only with its notice and the upstream commit recorded. MIT covers code, not characters: never publish Claude's Clawd mascot.

title: Never endorse or oppose a candidate in any CFC video
lesson: Never script a CFC video, or a video for churches to play, that endorses or opposes a candidate, and make church-safe cuts with no candidates and no criticism of officeholders. The Johnson Amendment still binds CFC.

title: Keep advocacy true and never automate hidden-AI messages
lesson: Make every advocacy claim true and sourced, never fake a grassroots movement, and never send automated messages to officials or voters at scale that hide their AI origin.

title: Never fake a real screen, document, or record
lesson: Show only real screenshots or generic interface elements; never mock up a real app, bill page, document, or record.

title: Commit after every verified item
lesson: Commit after each verified improvement, one item per commit, so the last commit is always a working video. Keep steps small in case a limit stops the session.

title: Keep a progress log and a handoff file
lesson: Keep PROGRESS.md (one row per item: what changed, images, checks, commit) and HANDOFF.md (goal, engine map, locked decisions, traps, commands) so any session can resume cold.

title: Never write in another session's folder; fork instead
lesson: One session owns a project folder. To change a delivered piece, fork it into a new folder and branch, and read the original only.

title: Turn a good first video into a skill, then a series
lesson: After a piece works, package its look, rules, and pipeline as a skill and reuse it for a series, so each episode keeps the same character, texture, and pacing.

title: Standardize one engine for production
lesson: Let Claude pick any stack for experiments, but standardize one engine for production so staff can learn it and edit it.

title: Plan for usage-limit stops mid-task
lesson: Expect long runs to hit usage limits: keep work committed, write progress as you go, and keep the session open so Claude Code can wait out a five-hour limit.

title: Plan every frame and sound as code
lesson: Plan every frame and every sound as code that CFC runs and owns: Claude has no native video, animation, audio, or music feature. Treat partner plugins in the marketplace as third-party tools under their own terms.

title: Freeze the contract, then give each worker one scene file
lesson: Freeze the engine, brief, and storyboard before parallel work. Each worker owns one scene file, keeps private helpers inside it, reports bugs in shared files instead of editing them, and guards every cross-scene handoff with a fallback.

title: Fold every fix back into the guide and the trap list
lesson: After each video, write a short review of what the model did well and badly, and turn each fix into a one-line trap or rule with the check that catches it. Carry the list into every new brief.

title: Carry a Banned list against Claude's house style
lesson: Put a Banned list in every brief: orange-dot-on-black openers, HUD corner labels, cream editorial pages with italic accent words, '01/02/03' labels, monospace captions, collage paper rips, constant wiggle, particle bursts, decorative glows, template chrome, and false mid-count numbers.

title: Aim for clarity and truth, not flash
lesson: Judge every scene by whether it makes the argument clearer. Cut tricks that show off the animation library without carrying a message.

title: Use code for text and numbers; real photos for people
lesson: Use code-rendered motion where text, numbers, logos, and timing must be exact, and real photos or footage where faces matter. Do not ask diffusion video for text.

title: Make fewer, excellent, well-sourced pieces
lesson: Invest in a few excellent, well-sourced flagships rather than many average pieces. Name the expert reviewers, state any measurement convention on screen, and finish the source sheet before release so the expected accuracy attack has an answer.

title: Put every scene on one persistent stage
lesson: Describe and draw one stage (a surface, a light, a camera) that every scene lives on, and move elements on and off it. Unrelated backgrounds per scene are the main reason scene 9 stops looking like scene 1.

title: Keep the visual spec and the motion spec apart
lesson: Write what a frame looks like (surfaces, palette, type, prohibitions) separately from how it moves (camera, entrances, rhythm, transitions). The look column holds no motion words; the motion column holds no colours.

title: Approve a rendered style frame before scene work
lesson: Before building scenes, render one still that shows the stage, palette, type, one hero shot per layout recipe, and the safe zones, and get it approved. It is the last cheap point to change the look, and every scene is then held to it.

title: One hero element at about 70 percent of the visual weight
lesson: Give each shot one dominant element (about 70 percent of the visual weight), two or three supporting elements at most, and generous empty space.

title: Reserve each accent colour and measure its share of the frame
